final_recommendation: The room converged on a comprehensive trilateral package with integrated enforcement: 70-72-75% RVC phase-in, 30-day labor wage-floor enforcement with real-time inspection access for all three countries, shared quarterly audit calendar with 45-day binding dispute resolution, six-year auto-renewal sunset with triple-veto mechanism, and five-year dairy tariff phase-down—all locked into main treaty articles at signature. Canada's Chapter 19 demand was rejected but offset by enforcement symmetry gains.
minority_objections: Canada initially demanded Chapter 19 dispute settlement remain in treaty text as precondition
USTR attempted to relegate RVC audit details and auto-renewal triggers to bilateral side letters rather than main treaty text
key_conflicts: Chapter 19 dispute settlement: Canada red line vs. U.S. Congressional rejection of pulling cases from U.S. courts
Enforcement sequencing: whether dairy, RVC, and sunset would be integrated in same treaty articles or sequential commitments
Labor verification access: Canada demanding same real-time inspection data as Mexico receives, not after-the-fact reports
Sunset mechanism design: whether auto-renewal defaults to continuation or resets to renegotiation uncertainty
key_concessions: Canada dropped Chapter 19 demand in exchange for labor enforcement symmetry and integrated treaty text
USTR abandoned bilateral side-letter approach, agreed to put all major provisions in main treaty articles
Mexico accepted shared trilateral audit calendar with binding 45-day dispute resolution
U.S. accepted six-year auto-renewal with triple-veto (any country can block) rather than hard sunset
Canada accepted five-year dairy tariff phase-down tied to labor enforcement timelines
red_lines: Canada: Real-time labor inspection access parity with Mexico (not reports after-the-fact)
Canada: All major provisions (dairy, RVC, sunset, Chapter 19 or equivalent enforcement) in main treaty text, not side letters
U.S. Congress: No Chapter 19 dispute settlement pulling U.S. cases from U.S. courts
U.S. Congress: Automatic 31-day tariff suspension for wage violations, no pattern-evidence requirement
Labor unions: Wage-floor enforcement triggers and timelines in main treaty articles with same legal weight as RVC
Auto industry: Integrated package at signature—no sequential dairy-after-autos or sunset-TBD commitments
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Political feasibility of Canada selling dairy concessions to domestic agricultural constituencies
Implementation capacity for real-time trilateral inspection data sharing across three regulatory systems
Risk that six-year auto-renewal with triple-veto creates recurring renegotiation leverage points
Supply-chain disruption during 70-72-75 phase-in if compliance verification proves more burdensome than anticipated
downstream_risk_variables: Congressional ratification timeline and political window before 2020 election
Canadian Parliamentary approval given dairy concessions without Chapter 19 protection
Mexican domestic labor law reform implementation to support $16/hour wage floor
Auto industry capital allocation decisions during three-year RVC phase-in period
Effectiveness of shared quarterly audit calendar in practice vs. theory
uncertainty_notes: Chapter 19 removal creates ongoing Canadian political vulnerability on dispute settlement. Auto-renewal mechanism with triple-veto may create recurring leverage points every six years rather than true stability. Real-time trilateral inspection data sharing has no tested precedent. Dairy concession scale and Canadian domestic ratification path remain unspecified.

marker_evidence.auto_rules_bottleneck: 75% RVC, phase-in timeline (70-72-75), and shared audit calendar with 45-day binding dispute resolution drove multiple rounds of negotiation and shaped final package structure—auto industry demanded glide path commitment before retooling, Mexico proposed breakthrough enforcement mechanism
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_key: 30-day wage-floor enforcement window, automatic day-31 tariff suspension, real-time inspection access parity, and integration into main treaty articles were explicitly tied to Congressional ratification throughout—Congress stated 'won't ratify if it looks like we gave Mexico a wage floor they can ignore,' labor unions demanded triggers 'in same treaty articles' as RVC
marker_evidence.canada_dairy_final_issue: Dairy market access and five-year tariff phase-down were Canada's stated precondition for trilateral signature, drove demand for integrated treaty text, and required parallel verification with labor enforcement—Canada said 'dairy opens, but tied to our labor verification' and USTR made it core concession demand
marker_evidence.dispute_settlement_canada_redline: Canada initially demanded Chapter 19 stay in treaty text as 'condition for Canada signing anything trilateral,' but ultimately dropped it in exchange for enforcement symmetry—raised as precondition but did not block final deal, so scored 1 not 2
marker_evidence.sunset_to_review_compromise: Hard sunset clause explicitly identified as 'business-uncertainty problem' that would 'freeze capital spending'—drove shift to six-year auto-renewal with triple-veto mechanism, supply-chain manufacturers stated 'won't retool $2B platforms if there's real risk Congress kills this in 2024,' auto-renewal compromise was decisive outcome
marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Congressional ratification constraints shaped multiple negotiation decisions: enforcement threshold demands, integrated-text requirements, rejection of Chapter 19, and timeline pressure—Congress repeatedly stated 'won't ratify' conditions that drove USTR positions and package structure
marker_evidence.supply_chain_adjustment: Raised as concern (retooling costs, $2B platform investments, phase-in needs) but did not change core outcomes—auto industry got requested 70-72-75 glide path, but this was accommodation not a concession that altered other parties' positions
marker_evidence.us_mexico_first_pressures_canada: U.S.-Mexico bilateral agreement on 75% RVC and wage floor was explicitly used as leverage—USTR told Canada 'Mexico's already locked in; you either match or we close this bilaterally,' Mexico stated 'that's our bilateral foundation, non-negotiable,' this pressure drove Canada's decision to accept package without Chapter 19
